source.title: Robustness study of noisy annotation in deep learning based medical image segmentation
source.authors: Shao-De Yu; Ming-Li Chen; Erlei Zhang; Jun-Jie Wu; Yu Hang; Zi Yang; Lin Ma; Xue-Jun Gu; Wei-Guo Lu

record.tranche_reason: Tests how varying the proportion of noisy annotations affects segmentation performance, using real clinical annotation noise rather than completely random labels.
record.gate_note: The study varies noisy-case proportions and reports training and test performance. It does not report results for shuffled or random labels, unstructured inputs, training time, explicit regularization, or learning order. Cited findings from Arpit et al. are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study measures segmentation with structured clinical annotation errors, not random labeling. Randomly selecting cases to retain rough annotations does not randomly corrupt their labels. Its results therefore test none of V1–V6; the learning-order explanation is attributed to Arpit et al., without an experiment measuring learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: segmentation is robust to noisy clinical annotations to some extent, but training with noisy annotations generally yields worse results than training with clean annotations. The authors also emphasize improving performance using limited clean samples.
record.recipe_differences: Uses real, imperfect clinical annotations in a medical segmentation task rather than completely random labels in the original classification settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with the proportion of noisy cases; test performance for 10% and 20% noisy cases was not significantly different from clean training.

fits_no_version.finding: Test DICE falls from 0.89±0.07 with clean annotations to 0.82±0.07 with all rough annotations; vs-FPR rises from 0.08±0.11 to 0.21±0.13. Differences from clean training are not significant at 10% or 20% noisy cases (p>0.25).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: HighRes3DNet tolerates modest proportions of rough clinical annotations in mandible CT segmentation, while larger proportions generally reduce test performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Training agreement with supplied annotations is imperfect, with DICE 0.80±0.09 at 10% noisy cases and 0.85±0.09 at 100%; agreement with clean annotations worsens as noisy-case proportions increase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training performance under structured clinical annotation errors depends on whether predictions are evaluated against supplied or corrected annotations.

record.problems: One task and one network architecture; only 12 test images; noise consists of real rough annotations rather than controlled random label corruption. Test-set results are mainly presented in a figure, and intermediate numerical values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 5 reports separate means for eight noisy-case percentages, but intermediate numerical values are figure-only and the supplied text does not state them; the trend and stated endpoints are captured in R1–R2. Figure 6 describes stable vs-FPR across proportions, but only the 10% and 100% values are stated in text; other proportions are not numerically extracted.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters under random labeling.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed as random corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error toward chance as random label corruption increases. Clinical annotation errors are a different manipulation.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and of removing these regularizers on true-label generalization.
Temporal ordering of learning shared patterns and memorizing noise; no separate learning trajectories are reported.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is warranted for the random-label claims. In particular, incomplete training agreement here does not challenge random-label memorization: the corruption mechanism differs, and the study does not establish training to full interpolation.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error under that labeling, and test error at chance.
Relative training time and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
The study varies proportions of real noisy annotations, not randomly corrupted labels; it does not report chance-level test error or perfect training fit across all noise proportions.
Whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent random-label fitting or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Learning order for real versus noisy or random labels; the discussion cites Arpit et al. but does not test this claim.

rows.subject: HighRes3DNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained with different percentages of cases carrying noisy annotations; selected models evaluated on the test set.

conditions.value: 0% to 60% at 10% increments and 100%; six random selections per percentage

rows.value: DICE values decreased as noisy cases increased; 100% noisy cases: 0.82±0.07
rows.uncertainty: Values reported as ±; two-sample t-test p>0.25 for 0% versus 10% or 20% noisy cases.
rows.note: Real annotation noise; intermediate values are not stated in text. The clean-versus-10%/20% test performance difference was not significant.
rows.check: The reported test DICE trend concerns rough clinical annotations, not V4's randomly corrupted labels. Even 100% noisy cases retain substantial anatomical signal. The numerical endpoints are supported.

rows.subject: HighRes3DNet
rows.operation_detail: Measured selected-model performance on training samples against the corresponding noisy labels.
rows.note: Training performance against noisy labels is not a measure of fit to clean labels or of random-label memorization.
rows.check: DICE 0.80±0.09 measures training predictions against the supplied annotations when 10% of cases retain rough annotations; it does not measure random-label fitting. Model selection is inconsistently described: Methods specifies minimum validation loss, whereas Results 3.2 specifies minimum training loss.

conditions.value: different percentages; endpoint percentages not explicitly paired with values in the sentence
